summary: For ages 12–14: treat a rounded value as an interval on the number line that is one rounding unit wide (half a unit on each side), compute lower and upper bounds as value ± half the rounding unit, and write error intervals with the correct inclusive/exclusive convention for round-half-up (lower bound included, upper bound excluded, e.g. 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5). Also use rounding to estimate calculation results and judge whether an estimate over- or under-shoots, comparing with the exact value when the rounding directions conflict. The central insight is that a single rounded number stands for a RANGE, and the upper end is excluded because at exactly halfway it would round up to the next value.
misconceptions: Treating a rounded measurement as exact (12 cm means exactly 12)
Using ± a whole unit rather than half a unit for the bounds
Getting the inclusive/exclusive symbols the wrong way round at the bounds
Assuming the upper bound is the rounded value itself (12.5 rounded to 12 but writing x ≤ 12)
Forgetting to halve the LAST place unit (nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05)

activities.title: Bounds explorer on a number line
steps: Enter a rounded value and its rounding unit (e.g. 12 to the nearest cm).
Mark on a number line a closed point at the lower bound (11.5) and an open point at the upper bound (12.5), labelling the interval 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5.
Place a 'true measurement' marker anywhere inside the bracket and check it stays within the half-unit each side.
Drag the true marker to the open upper end and reason about what happens: 12.5 would round up to 13, so it is excluded from this interval.
Change the rounding unit to 'nearest 10' and redraw the bracket at ±5; try 'nearest 0.1' and redraw at ±0.05.
activities.insight: A single rounded number really stands for an interval one rounding unit wide, with half a unit on EACH side; the upper bound is the excluded (open) end of the bracket because exactly halfway rounds up to the next value.

activities.title: Writing and checking error intervals
steps: Write the error interval for a length of 24 cm measured to the nearest cm, using inequality notation.
State the lower and upper bounds separately and choose the correct symbol at each end.
Answer: for a mass given as 5 kg to the nearest kg, what is the smallest it could be?
Explain why the top bound uses < and not ≤ by saying what that top value would round to.
activities.insight: Bounds are value ± half the rounding unit, and the two ends use different symbols: the lower bound is included (it rounds up into the value) and the upper bound is excluded (it would round up to the next value).

activities.title: Estimate by rounding and judge over/under
steps: Estimate 61.2 × 3.9 by rounding each factor sensibly, then check against the exact value to say whether your estimate is over or under the true answer, noting which factor was rounded up and which down.
Estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding each factor to one significant figure, and state what you rounded each number to.
Compare your estimate with the exact value to find the direction of the error, and explain why the rounding alone could not tell you the direction when one factor was rounded up and the other down.
activities.insight: Rounding each value to a convenient figure gives a quick reasonableness check; when both positive factors round the same way the over/under direction of the product is clear, but when they round in opposite directions you must compare with the exact value to see the actual direction.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch the working: 'A length is measured as 24 cm to the nearest centimetre. Write its error interval using inequalities. Then estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding, and say what you rounded each number to.' Watch the bounds and the inequality signs.
checkAnswer: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5 (lower bound 23.5, upper bound 24.5); and about 400 × 6 = 2400.
